imported-teak-guide.title: Imported Teak Wood: African Origins, Quality and Buying Advice
imported-teak-guide.excerpt: Buying imported or African teak? Learn how to verify true teak, assess grade and seasoning, and compare timber for doors, windows and frames.
imported-teak-guide.summary: Buying imported or African teak? Learn how to verify true teak, assess grade and seasoning, and compare timber for doors, windows and frames.
paragraphs: Two bundles sold as imported teak can look similar and behave differently in a finished door. Before comparing their price, establish what the wood is, where it came from and how much usable, properly conditioned timber the bundle contains.

This is especially important with “African teak”. The name may describe genuine teak grown in Africa, but it is also used for unrelated timbers. A country name is useful sourcing information; it is not a quality grade.

sections.title: Is African teak real teak?

blocks.text: True teak is Tectona grandis. It is native to parts of South and Southeast Asia and has been planted in other tropical regions, including Africa. Plantation-grown Tectona grandis is genuine teak regardless of the country where it grows.

However, “African teak” is also a common name for Iroko, including Milicia excelsa. Iroko and true teak are different woods. Do not transfer teak's properties to a board simply because a seller uses the word teak.

Ask for Tectona grandis on the specification when that is the material you intend to buy. Where identification remains uncertain on a significant order, specialist testing is more dependable than judging a photograph or colour sample.

sections.title: Where does imported teak come from?

blocks.text: Teak plantations have been established in countries including Ghana, Nigeria, Côte d'Ivoire, Togo, Benin and Tanzania, as well as countries outside Africa. The available source depends on the supplier and consignment.
Distinguish the place where the tree grew from the country through which it was shipped. Neither a port name nor a trading label establishes the harvest origin by itself.
Imported teak and plantation teak are overlapping descriptions: the first describes trade across a border, while the second describes how the trees were grown. Neither term specifies a uniform grade.

sections.title: What determines the quality of imported teak?

blocks.text: Heartwood and usable dimensions
Ask how much sound heartwood is available in the lengths and widths your design needs. Sapwood should be assessed separately rather than assumed to have the same natural durability as teak heartwood.

A large-looking log or wide rough board can lose a substantial amount of usable material when defects and sapwood are removed. For doors and frames, compare finished usable sections, not just the outside dimensions of the timber.
Grain, colour and defects

Teak can vary from lighter golden-brown tones to darker brown, with differences between pieces and surfaces. Grain may be straight or less regular. Look at uncoated, prepared samples from the actual stock.

Inspect knots, splits, bends and damaged areas in relation to the components to be cut. Attractive figure on a panel does not make a defective hinge stile acceptable. For double doors, agree on how colour and grain will be matched across both leaves.
Growing conditions and tree age
Plantation site, management, individual trees and processing can affect the resulting timber. A country label or a claimed age is not enough to judge a board.

Do not assume that all fast-grown teak is unsuitable, or that any timber over a particular age is automatically premium. Ask for the measurable qualities your product needs: sound usable size, appropriate heartwood, acceptable defects and correct condition.
Moisture and storage
Transport time is not a seasoning certificate. Imported timber can gain or lose moisture during storage and handling, so its condition should be checked before machining.

Ask for current moisture readings and how they were obtained. The target should suit the product and its service environment; there is no single percentage for every indoor and outdoor application. Correct meter settings and representative measurements matter more than one impressive-looking reading.

sections.title: Seasoning imported teak for joinery

blocks.text: Both air drying and kiln drying can form part of timber preparation. What matters is the result: suitable moisture, reasonably uniform condition, manageable drying stresses and freedom from unacceptable drying defects.

Boards should remain protected and appropriately stored after drying. Poor storage can undo part of the benefit of careful conditioning. “Seasoned abroad” and “stored for years” should lead to questions about present condition, not end the inspection.
A manufacturer should plan selection, drying, machining and assembly together. Clearances, panel construction and joint design must allow for normal wood movement.

sections.title: Uses for doors, windows, frames and furniture

blocks.text: Doors
Suitable imported Tectona grandis can be used for solid-wood and panelled doors. Choose stock for the design, and assess the frame, joints and hardware as part of the finished assembly.

For an entrance exposed to rain and strong sunlight, agree on protection and maintenance before selecting the finish. An unfinished display sample is useful for evaluating the wood, but it does not define the final exterior specification.
Windows and chaukhat

Windows need attention to drainage, joints, end grain and coating. Chaukhat needs sound, straight sections and suitable fixing positions. In both cases, specify the finished dimensions after machining rather than relying only on a rough-sawn size.
Furniture and decorative work
Grain selection, panel layout and finishing often have a greater visual role in furniture. Agree on whether natural colour variation is welcome or whether a more consistent appearance is required.

Teak's natural extractives can influence adhesive and coating performance. The manufacturer should use compatible products and the preparation recommended by their manufacturers, with a sample finish approved before the full order.

sections.title: Is imported teak termite-proof?

blocks.text: No timber should be sold with an unrestricted promise that it can never suffer insect or fungal damage. Teak heartwood is valued for natural durability, but sapwood, material quality and exposure still matter.

Keep timber away from avoidable persistent damp, specify suitable construction details and address any site-specific protection needs. A timber's reputation does not replace an inspection or a sensible maintenance plan.

sections.title: Defects to check before buying

blocks.text: Inspect more than the outer boards in a bundle. Ask to see the stock selected for your order and assess defects where joints, hinges or lock recesses will be cut.

rows: Can cause later shrinkage, movement and poor fit.
Reduce usable size and can affect joints.
Can interfere with appearance, machining and local strength.
Can prevent required straight components being cut.
Especially difficult in long stiles and frame sections.
Do not assume teak heartwood's natural durability.
Assess deterioration; staining alone is not the same as decay.
Check the extent and remaining sound material.
Can leave moisture gradients or drying stresses.
May not yield the agreed dimensions after machining.

blocks.text: A feature that can be removed as an offcut may be acceptable. One that remains in a critical finished component needs a different decision. Agree on the allowed grade and replacement process before production.

sections.title: Imported African teak vs Indian or Nigam teak

blocks.text: When both are correctly identified as Tectona grandis, they are the same species. Their source, dimensions, grade and condition can still differ.

“Nigam teak” describes a forest-corporation sales channel; it does not independently prove a particular tree age, forest origin or quality grade. Compare the actual lots and records rather than treating imported and Nigam as two fixed quality categories.

Indian source and sale channel; verify records
Depends on supplier and international supply
Depends on supplier, lots and regional supply
Varies within countries, plantations and lots
Varies within regions, trees and lots
Supplier and source records for the consignment

sections.title: Price and value: compare the complete order

blocks.text: Country of origin, available dimensions, grade, freight, currency movements, seasoning and processing can influence imported-timber costs. A current quote for the actual lot is more useful than a generic price list.

Ask whether the rate is per cubic foot of rough timber, per finished section or per completed product. Include machining loss, joints, hardware, finishing, transport and installation when comparing door quotations.
A lower rough-timber rate can become expensive if many pieces fail to yield the required finished size. Conversely, paying more for a prestige origin does not remove the need to inspect the material.

sections.title: Source records and responsible purchasing

blocks.text: Request an invoice with the agreed timber identity, stated origin, dimensions and grade. Where available, keep relevant sourcing records that support the supplier's description.

If certification is claimed, check that the claim applies to the supplied product and its chain of custody. Imported wood is not automatically certified, and plantation-grown timber is not automatically proof of responsible management.
Do not treat a generic certificate, a shipping-country label or a photograph of logs as proof for every batch.

sections.title: Discuss an imported teak project with NORDWOOD

blocks.text: For doors, windows or frames in Lucknow, bring the opening dimensions, your preferred design and details of site exposure. Compare the actual stock and an unpolished sample during a workshop visit, then agree on the material and finish in writing.
NORDWOOD offers on-site consultation, workshop visits and free installation. Confirm the finished sizes and hardware in the quotation so the price relates to a clear product specification.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions

blocks.text: Are imported teak and African teak the same?
No. Imported teak may come from several regions. African teak is an ambiguous trade name, so verify whether the timber is Tectona grandis or another species.
Is Ghana teak genuine teak?
Teak grown in Ghana can be Tectona grandis. The country name alone does not prove the identity or grade of a particular consignment.
Is imported teak inferior to Indian teak?
There is no reliable blanket ranking. Compare the actual species, grade, heartwood, usable dimensions, defects and seasoning.
Does imported teak need seasoning?
It needs to be in suitable condition for manufacture and service. Even previously dried timber should be checked after transport and storage.
How do I check whether the timber is genuine?
Start with a clear written specification and supporting records. Visual inspection is helpful but not conclusive; use specialist identification when necessary.
Can imported teak be used for an exterior main door?
Suitable stock can be used with appropriate design, joinery, finish and maintenance. Assess the actual rain and sunlight exposure.
What should I ask before paying?
Confirm species, source description, grade, finished dimensions, moisture condition and the complete scope of manufacture and installation.

sources.title: FAO overview of teak — explains the species' native range and establishment beyond it.
FAO teak plantation reference — discusses how site and plantation conditions influence growth and wood characteristics.
NCBI entry for Milicia excelsa — records African teak as a common name for a species distinct from Tectona grandis.
USDA Wood Handbook: drying and dimensional change — explains conditioning timber for service.

plantation-teak-guide.title: Plantation Teak Wood: Quality, Uses and What to Check Before Buying
plantation-teak-guide.excerpt: Is plantation teak right for your doors or frames? Learn how to assess heartwood, grain, seasoning, sourcing and price before choosing timber.
plantation-teak-guide.summary: Is plantation teak right for your doors or frames? Learn how to assess heartwood, grain, seasoning, sourcing and price before choosing timber.
paragraphs: Plantation teak can be a good choice for a wooden door, window or chaukhat. The useful question is not whether plantation wood is automatically better or worse than forest teak. It is whether the actual timber has the right heartwood, dimensions, condition and preparation for your project.
The name describes how the trees were grown. It does not tell you the grade of the boards, their moisture content or how well a finished door will be made.

sections.title: What is plantation teak?

blocks.text: Plantation teak is Tectona grandis grown in planted stands. It is the same species as genuine teak from natural forests, commonly called sagwan in India.

Teak is planted in India and many other tropical countries. African sources include Ghana, Benin, Togo, Nigeria, Côte d'Ivoire and Tanzania; plantations also exist in parts of Southeast Asia and Latin America. FAO's work on teak plantation management describes how site conditions and management affect the resource.
A plantation can supply good joinery timber, but the label alone does not demonstrate responsible management or a traceable supply chain.

sections.title: Plantation teak, forest teak and imported teak are different descriptions

blocks.text: “Plantation” and “natural forest” describe growing origin. “Imported” describes a supply route. A board can therefore be both plantation teak and imported teak.
“Nigam teak” usually points to a forest-corporation sales channel. “Burma teak” is a geographical trade description and should not be used as a synonym for every piece of old or forest-grown teak.
At the board level, compare sound heartwood, defects, usable section size, grain and drying quality. Neither wider growth rings nor a darker colour proves that one piece will outperform another.

sections.title: What does plantation teak look like?

blocks.text: Teak heartwood commonly ranges from golden-brown to brown, sometimes with darker streaks. The outer sapwood is usually paler. Grain can be straight, wavy or more strongly figured, and neighbouring boards need not match exactly.
A striking grain pattern may be ideal for a visible panel. A straighter piece may be a better choice for a long frame member. The cutting direction also changes what the grain looks like.
Ask to see an unpolished sample and a finished sample of the proposed timber. Stain, surface preparation and lighting can make the same wood look surprisingly different.

sections.title: What matters more than a promised tree age?

blocks.text: Sound heartwood

Teak heartwood is valued for natural durability. Sapwood should not be assumed to have the same resistance. Ask how much sapwood will be included and where it will be used, particularly in exposed components.
Heartwood content matters, but it does not excuse deep cracks, decay or poorly placed knots.
Grain and usable dimensions
Check the full length of boards for twist, bow, splits and defects. A large rough section may yield a much smaller sound, finished component.
For doors, ask which boards will form the stiles, rails and panels. For frames, check the finished section after rebates and machining.
Moisture condition
Wood keeps responding to humidity after installation. Teak generally moves less than many timbers, but it is not motionless and cannot be guaranteed never to bind, split or open at a joint.

Avoid a universal “8–12% is right for everything” rule. The target should suit the end use and service environment, with readings checked across the relevant timber. BIS IS 287 provides purpose- and climate-related recommendations.
Age and source records
A harvest-age claim is useful only when it is supported and interpreted alongside the timber itself. There is no universal age threshold at which plantation teak becomes suitable for every door.
Young and mature stands can differ in heartwood and wood characteristics, but site, genetics, management, defects and processing also matter. Ask what can actually be documented.

sections.title: Where plantation teak can work well

blocks.text: Wooden doors
Properly selected timber can suit panelled entrance doors, internal doors and decorative joinery. The construction must allow movement, and the hinges and fixings must suit the leaf's weight.
A sheltered entrance and an exposed entrance need different protection. A durable species does not remove the need for a suitable coating and good installation.
Wooden windows

For windows, assess the complete system: timber selection, frame and sash dimensions, glazing, seals, drainage and hardware. Teak's useful dimensional behaviour can help, but it does not automatically justify slimmer sections or larger panes.
Those dimensions need to be designed for the actual opening and loads.
Door frames and chaukhats
A chaukhat must remain straight and hold its fixings securely. Look for suitable long sections, sound areas around joints and hinges, and a moisture condition appropriate for installation.
Keep frame-to-masonry and floor junctions detailed to limit persistent wetting. A timber label cannot compensate for a damp opening or poor fixing.
Furniture and other woodwork
Plantation teak is also used in furniture and decorative work. Whether a particular board is suitable depends on its grade, size and intended exposure.

sections.title: How it compares with other materials

blocks.text: Plantation teak and Indian sal

Sal is Shorea robusta, a different species. Its substantial weight and strength can suit frames and other demanding uses, while teak is valued for its combination of appearance, workability and dimensional behaviour. Both need appropriate preparation; compare the actual quotation and timber rather than declaring one universally superior.
Plantation teak and sheesham

Sheesham, commonly Dalbergia sissoo, is valued for its distinctive figure and furniture applications. Compare grade, seasoning, dimensions and exposure for a door project. Attractive grain alone does not establish exterior suitability.
Plantation teak and mahogany
“Mahogany” can cover different botanical groups. Confirm the identity before comparing movement or decay resistance. Broad claims that all mahogany is only for interiors are unhelpful.
Plantation teak and pine

Pine covers many species and grades. Some softwoods are used successfully in joinery with appropriate design, treatment and coatings. Teak's natural durability and appearance may justify a higher price for some projects, but assess the complete specification.
Plantation teak and engineered doors

Plywood, MDF, laminated timber and engineered door assemblies are not interchangeable. Their cores, adhesives, grades and finishes differ. Properly specified engineered products can be suitable for their rated applications; ordinary MDF is not a fair stand-in for the whole category.

sections.title: Is plantation teak sustainable?

blocks.text: It can form part of a responsible supply chain, but plantation origin alone is not proof. Ask about the source, land management and traceability, and verify any certification claim against the relevant supplier and product.
Certification and quality answer different questions. A certified board still needs to be checked for grade and moisture; an attractive board does not establish how its source was managed.

sections.title: What affects the price?

blocks.text: Price reflects the available dimensions, usable heartwood, defects, grade, drying and processing, as well as origin and supply costs. Larger clear sections may be more valuable than smaller pieces with the same nominal volume.
For a finished door, include machining, joinery, finish, hardware, delivery and installation in the comparison. No general article can give a reliable current price for every specification.

When comparing rough timber, confirm the volume calculation. For rectangular sections measured in inches with length in feet, cubic feet = thickness × width × length ÷ 144. Use consistent units and clarify whether the quoted dimensions are rough or finished.

sections.title: Caring for plantation teak joinery

blocks.text: Clean gently and follow the instructions for the actual finish. Do not add teak oil, polish or wax simply because the wood is teak; it may not suit the existing coating.

Check exposed edges, joints, glazing seals and areas around hardware. Repair worn coatings and water-entry points promptly. Recoating intervals depend on exposure and the chosen system, so a fixed “every one or two years” rule is not suitable for every installation.
Untreated teak can change colour outdoors, but surface greying does not prove that every underlying joint or timber section remains sound.

sections.title: Questions buyers often ask

blocks.text: Is plantation teak genuine teak?
Yes, when it is Tectona grandis. “Plantation” describes cultivation, not an alternative species.
Is plantation teak termite-proof?
No. Heartwood has natural resistance, but the timber, sapwood content and exposure vary. Termite management and moisture control still matter.
How long will a plantation teak door last?
There is no responsible universal lifespan. Timber quality, construction, exposure, coating and maintenance all affect service life. Ask what warranty applies to the specific product.
Is forest teak always better?
No. Compare the particular grade and boards. Origin and age alone cannot establish finished-product performance.
Can I order an unpolished teak door?
NORDWOOD offers unpolished as well as polished products. Agree the storage and finishing plan so the door is protected before service.

sections.title: Choosing plantation teak with NORDWOOD

blocks.text: If you are planning custom doors, windows or chaukhats in Lucknow, bring your design and opening details to NORDWOOD. Compare the available timber in person and discuss the finished sizes, exposure and finish before confirming the order.
The best specification is one you can understand and check: identified timber, suitable sections, appropriate moisture condition and clear details for manufacture and installation.

sources.title: FAO — Management of Teak Plantations
USDA Forest Products Laboratory — Wood Handbook
BIS — IS 287 moisture-content recommendations

malaysian-saal-guide.title: Malaysian Sal Wood: What It Is and How to Buy It for Doors and Frames
malaysian-saal-guide.excerpt: Understand Malaysian Sal wood, how it differs from Indian Sal, and what to check for doors, windows and chaukhat before comparing prices.
malaysian-saal-guide.summary: Understand Malaysian Sal wood, how it differs from Indian Sal, and what to check for doors, windows and chaukhat before comparing prices.
paragraphs: A quotation that says “Malaysian Sal” leaves an important question unanswered: which timber are you buying? In the Indian market, this name can refer to imported hardwood sold under a broad trade label. It does not identify one wood with a fixed set of properties.

Before comparing rates for a door, window or chaukhat, ask for the recognised commercial timber group or botanical species. That one detail makes the discussion about strength, durability and value much more useful.

sections.title: What does Malaysian Sal mean?

blocks.text: Indian forestry research has used “Malaysian Sal” for imported Meranti timber. For example, an ICFRE report identifies material described as Golden Teak or Malaysian Sal with the Yellow Meranti group. Malaysian timber references distinguish recognised groups such as Yellow Meranti, Light Red Meranti and Dark Red Meranti.

These group names are more informative than an informal market label, although a commercial group may still contain several species. Ask the supplier which specification applies to the stock being offered. A description copied from another Meranti group is not sufficient.
Is Malaysian Sal the same as Indian Sal?

Indian Sal, also called Sakhu or Saakhu, is Shorea robusta. Do not assume that imported timber sold as Malaysian Sal is the same species. Kapur, sometimes marketed as Kapoor Sal, is another separate timber group.
The comparison below explains what can reasonably be said before the imported timber has been identified.

rows: Verify the species or recognised timber group
Imported timber sold under a market label
Use the identified Meranti or other verified group
Depends on timber group and surface condition
Group-dependent; Meranti is often moderately coarse
Use data for the identified group
Generally heavy; varies within the species
Assess the identified timber and exposure
Joinery where the identified timber is suitable

sections.title: Colour, grain and texture

blocks.text: There is no single Malaysian Sal colour. Meranti groups can differ considerably: the yellow-brown appearance associated with Yellow Meranti is different from the pinkish or reddish-brown colours of Red Meranti groups.

Look at an uncoated, freshly prepared surface in daylight. A polished sample can make the colour look deeper and conceal the appearance you will receive in an unfinished frame. Interlocked grain can produce attractive figure, but it can also demand care when planing and profiling.
Compare the actual pieces allocated to the order. Matching colour across a double door is a separate selection task from finding sound timber for a concealed frame.

sections.title: Density and strength: use the right specification

blocks.text: A single density or bending-strength value cannot describe everything sold as Malaysian Sal. Technical data belong to the named timber group and test conditions; they are not a guarantee for an individual board.

For a door, the practical questions are its weight, the quality of the joints, and the timber around hinges and locks. For a chaukhat, long straight sections and sound fixing positions matter. A dense piece with a deep split beside a hinge recess is a poor choice despite its weight.
Ask the manufacturer to specify the finished section for the opening and shutter load. Ordinary joinery advice should not be used as a structural design specification.

sections.title: Durability, termites and outdoor exposure

blocks.text: Check durability against the identified timber and its intended use. Heartwood and sapwood can perform differently, and indoor service is different from repeated rain exposure or contact with damp masonry.

Avoid blanket promises that Malaysian Sal is termite-proof, rot-proof or maintenance-free. Where protection is needed, ask for a suitable treatment and finishing specification, including its limitations. Surface polish alone is not proof of termite protection.

For an exposed window, design also matters: water must drain away, joints need protection, and the coating must be maintained. Timber selection cannot compensate for a detail that repeatedly traps water.

sections.title: Seasoning and moisture before manufacture

blocks.text: Wood takes up and releases moisture as its surroundings change. If the timber is poorly conditioned when it is machined, later movement can affect door clearances, frame alignment and joints.

Air drying and kiln drying are methods, not quality grades. Ask how the supplier checked the result: measured moisture, consistency through the stock, drying defects and storage after drying. A claim that boards have been stored for years does not establish their present condition.

There is no one moisture percentage for every building. The target should suit the installation environment and end use. A surface reading should also be interpreted with the meter settings and timber thickness in mind.

sections.title: Where can Malaysian Sal be used?

blocks.text: Doors

Identified, appropriately selected material may be suitable for doors. Agree on the design, exposure and finish before buying. Inspect stiles and rails for defects around joints, and allow for panel movement in the construction.
For large or double doors, specify suitable hinges and the meeting detail between leaves. Simply enlarging a small-door design can change its weight and demands on the frame.
Windows

Some Meranti groups are established joinery timbers, but an outdoor window still needs a group-specific suitability assessment. Check the profiles, drainage, joints and coating as a complete specification.
Chaukhat and frames

Focus on straightness, finished dimensions, sound fixing areas and moisture condition. A nominal rough-sawn size is not necessarily the size left after planing, rebating and removing defects. Ask for the finished width and depth in writing.

sections.title: What to inspect before ordering

items: Identity: the recognised timber group or botanical species, not only the name Malaysian Sal.
Source: the stated origin and supporting supplier records.
Grade: the agreed allowance for knots, sapwood, splits and other defects.
Condition: current moisture readings, drying method and storage.
Straightness: sight along the length and check for bow, crook, cup and twist.
Surface and ends: inspect cracks, insect holes, soft areas and signs of decay.
Usable size: confirm finished dimensions, lengths and expected machining loss.
Product specification: agree on joints, hardware, finish and installation.

blocks.text: Colour alone cannot reliably identify a timber. For a high-value order with uncertain identification, specialist wood-anatomy testing is more useful than an online photo comparison.

sections.title: Malaysian Sal vs Sal, teak and Sheesham

blocks.text: Compare material suitable for the same product and exposure. The table gives buying considerations, not a universal ranking of woods.

sections.title: Price: compare the finished requirement

blocks.text: A low rate per cubic foot is useful only when the identity, grade and measurement basis are clear. Ask whether the quote covers rough timber, machined sections or the completed product.

Allow for seasoning, sorting, planing, waste, joinery, hardware, finishing, delivery and installation. Import and transport costs can also affect the price of Malaysian timber. Obtain a current quotation for the actual specification rather than treating an online rate as a fixed market price.

sections.title: Sourcing and certification

blocks.text: Imported timber is not automatically certified or sustainably sourced. Where a certification claim is made, ask for the applicable product claim and supply-chain documentation. Malaysia has a timber certification scheme, but that does not make every Malaysian consignment certified.
Keep the invoice and written material specification. If the agreed timber changes, approve the substitution before manufacture.

sections.title: Choosing material with NORDWOOD

blocks.text: For a project in Lucknow, bring the opening dimensions, a design reference and information about rain or sunlight exposure to NORDWOOD. A workshop visit helps you compare the actual timber, unfinished samples and construction details before deciding.

NORDWOOD offers on-site consultation, workshop visits and free installation. Use the quotation to record the timber, finished sizes, hardware and finish so that the completed work can be checked against the order.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions

blocks.text: Is Malaysian Sal good for chaukhat?
It can be considered when the actual timber is identified and appropriate for the frame. Sound sections, seasoning, dimensions and fixing details must be checked together.
Is Malaysian Sal better than Indian Sal?
The market name is too broad for that conclusion. Compare the identified imported timber with the actual Shorea robusta stock, using the same product requirements and grade.
Can I identify it by its colour?
Colour is a useful observation, but it is not reliable proof of species. Finishes, exposure and differences within a timber group can change its appearance.
Is old stock always better?
No. Storage age does not prove correct moisture, good seasoning or freedom from defects. Inspect and measure the timber as it is supplied.
Can it be used outdoors?
Only with a suitable timber specification and design for the exposure. Confirm any required treatment, coating and maintenance.
What should my quotation call the wood?
Ask for the recognised commercial timber group or botanical species alongside the market name, with origin, grade and finished dimensions where applicable.

sources.title: ICFRE research on imported timber — provides an example of Malaysian Sal being used as a market name for Yellow Meranti.
Malaysian Timber Council technical references — distinguish commercial timber groups and their properties.
USDA Wood Handbook: drying and dimensional change — explains moisture conditioning and wood movement.
Malaysian Timber Certification Council — explains timber certification and chain of custody.

desi-sal-guide.title: Sal Wood (Sakhu): A Practical Guide for Doors, Windows and Chaukhat
desi-sal-guide.excerpt: Learn how to assess Sal or Sakhu wood for doors, windows and chaukhat, including seasoning, defects, regional sourcing and comparisons with teak.
desi-sal-guide.summary: Learn how to assess Sal or Sakhu wood for doors, windows and chaukhat, including seasoning, defects, regional sourcing and comparisons with teak.
paragraphs: A chaukhat has a demanding job: it carries the shutter, holds the hinges and keeps the opening square through daily use. Sal is a familiar choice for this work in northern India, but its reputation is only the starting point. The quality of the selected sections and their seasoning matter just as much.
If you are buying Sal for a home in Lucknow or comparing supplies from Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand, inspect the actual timber before deciding by region or price.

sections.title: What is Sal wood?

blocks.text: Indian Sal is Shorea robusta. It is also called Sakhu, Saakhu or Sakhua; spellings vary between markets. It is a different species from teak, or Sagwan, which is Tectona grandis.

The names Malaysian Sal and Kapoor Sal should not be treated as alternative names for Shorea robusta. They can refer to other imported timbers. Ask the seller to put the timber identity on the quotation so you can compare like with like.

sections.title: Appearance, grain and weight

blocks.text: Sal is generally a hard, heavy timber. Its heartwood is brown and can darken with exposure, while the sapwood is usually paler. Grain is often interlocked and the texture medium to coarse; a prepared surface may show ribbon-like figure.

These are useful characteristics, not a reliable identification test on their own. Colour varies with the piece, surface preparation, lighting and finish. A stained sample can look very different from an unpolished section.

For a visible door, compare the grain and colour across the selected components. For a concealed frame, straightness and sound timber around joints and fixings deserve more attention than decorative grain.

sections.title: Is Sal suitable for chaukhat?

blocks.text: Sal can be a practical choice for door frames when the material is sound, properly conditioned and suitable for the design. Long sections need to be straight, and the hinge and lock areas should be free of defects that interfere with the work.

Confirm the finished frame size after planing and rebating. Buying a nominal rough section does not guarantee that the finished frame will retain those dimensions. The required section also depends on the opening, shutter weight, joint design and fixing method.
Heavy doors need suitable hinges, fixings and a frame installation that transfers the load correctly. Wood hardness alone cannot prevent problems caused by poor installation.

sections.title: Sal wood for doors and windows

blocks.text: Solid wooden doors

Sal can be used in suitable door construction, but its weight and working characteristics need to be considered. The design should accommodate moisture movement, especially in wide panels, and the hardware should suit the finished shutter.
A double door also needs a planned meeting detail, clearances and reliable alignment. Do not judge the specification only by the appearance of a small sample.
Windows

For windows, timber selection is one part of the specification. Exterior joinery also needs appropriate profiles, drainage, protected joints and a suitable finish. Repeated wetting at a sill or an unprotected end can undermine otherwise sound workmanship.
A protected interior opening and a window exposed to monsoon rain should not receive the same recommendation without assessing the site.

sections.title: Durability and termite resistance

blocks.text: Sal heartwood is valued for durability, but that does not mean every piece is termite-proof or decay-proof. Sapwood, damaged timber and persistently damp conditions need separate attention.

Inspect for insect holes, soft areas and signs of decay. Ask what treatment, if any, has been specified for the actual exposure and material. Treatment claims should describe a real process; neither a dark colour nor a coat of polish proves protection.
For outdoor use, limit prolonged wetting through design and maintain the finish. Follow the coating manufacturer's instructions and inspect vulnerable edges and joints as the product ages.

sections.title: Why careful seasoning matters

blocks.text: Sal requires care during drying. A dry-looking surface can hide uneven moisture or drying stresses, and aggressive drying can lead to checking or distortion. Do not confuse a timber's strength with an ability to ignore seasoning.

Ask the manufacturer to check moisture before machining and again as appropriate during production. Moisture-meter readings need suitable settings and interpretation for the species, section and testing method.

There is no single percentage that suits every building. The target should reflect the end use and service environment; BIS IS 287 provides Indian recommendations for timber moisture content for different uses.
Does older wood mean better wood?

The age of the tree and the time boards have spent in storage are different things. Neither is a complete quality grade. An old board stored in damp conditions may still be unsuitable, while appropriately dried and well-selected stock may perform well without a dramatic age claim.
Ask for evidence of condition, rather than relying on “old” or “fully seasoned” as unmeasured descriptions.

sections.title: What to inspect in Sal timber

blocks.text: Check several pieces from the batch, including the ends and the full length. A good-looking face should not distract from a split, bend or defect where a joint must be cut.

rows: Later movement can change fit and alignment.
Can reduce usable size and weaken a joint area.
Can interfere with machining, joints and appearance.
A bend along the face affects long components.
An edgewise bend makes straight sections difficult.
Corners fall out of plane; a particular problem for frames.
Curvature across the width reduces usable thickness.
Assess the extent and whether sound timber remains.
Soft or deteriorated timber can lose strength.
Do not assume the durability of selected heartwood.

blocks.text: A defect's location matters. A small feature in a removable offcut may be acceptable; the same feature at a hinge, tenon or narrow frame section may not be. Agree on the usable grade before manufacture.

sections.title: Sal from Uttar Pradesh vs Uttarakhand

blocks.text: Both regional descriptions can refer to Shorea robusta. They do not establish a quality ranking. Growing conditions, individual trees, conversion, grade and drying create differences within either supply.
Also distinguish where a log grew from the depot where it was sold. Ask what the available records actually establish instead of assuming that a depot location proves forest origin.

rows: Verify origin separately from sale depot
Verify origin separately from sale depot
Measure and condition for end use
Measure and condition for end use

sections.title: Sal wood price: ask for a comparable quotation

blocks.text: Sal prices depend on grade, dimensions, available lengths, seasoning, supply and processing. A rough-timber rate is not the same as a completed-frame price.

Ask whether measurement is based on rough or finished dimensions, and allow for material lost in sawing, planing and removing defects. For a completed product, compare the timber specification, joints, hardware, finish, delivery and installation together.
Keep the material description and source records with the invoice. Where certification or a particular origin is claimed, ask for supporting documents rather than relying on a general assurance.

sections.title: Sal vs teak for doors and frames

blocks.text: Both woods can be useful in joinery, but the choice should follow the application, actual grade, exposure, appearance and budget. Teak's reputation does not make every teak board superior to every Sal board; equally, Sal's hardness does not settle the comparison.

rows: Parts of South and Southeast Asia
Generally hard and heavy; grade matters
Variable; select to suit appearance and work

sections.title: Ordering Sal doors or frames with NORDWOOD

blocks.text: Start with the opening measurements, shutter design and site conditions. At a workshop visit, compare the actual Sal stock and an unfinished sample, then agree on the finished sections and surface finish.
NORDWOOD offers on-site consultation, workshop visits and free installation. Record the material, dimensions, hardware and finish in the order so that the agreed product is clear before manufacture.

Before accepting installation, check that the frame is square, the shutter moves freely and the hardware is secure. Ask how to care for the selected finish and who to contact if an adjustment is needed.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions

blocks.text: Are Sal and Sakhu the same wood?
In this guide, both names refer to Indian Sal, Shorea robusta. Confirm that identity with the supplier because informal market names can be ambiguous.
Is Sal good for door frames?
It can be suitable when the sections are sound, correctly sized, properly conditioned and installed for the intended door.
Is Uttarakhand Sal always better than UP Sal?
No dependable quality ranking follows from the regional name alone. Compare the actual grade, straightness, defects and moisture condition.
Will a Sal door warp?
Any solid wood can move as moisture changes. Suitable selection, drying, storage, construction and installation reduce the risk; no timber name guarantees zero movement.
Can I leave Sal unpolished?
An unfinished sample shows the natural surface, but the final protection should suit the use and exposure. If you want a natural look, test a compatible finish on an offcut before approving it.
Can I judge quality by weight?
Weight is only one observation and is affected by moisture and dimensions. It does not prove species, seasoning or usable grade.
Is Sal cheaper than teak?
Often it is considered as a cost alternative, but the actual comparison needs current quotations for equivalent grade, dimensions and completed work. Do not assume a fixed price difference.

sources.title: ICFRE field identification handbook — describes the identity and anatomical characteristics of Shorea robusta.
BIS IS 287: timber moisture recommendations — provides the Indian standard reference for different timber uses.
USDA Wood Handbook — covers wood moisture, drying, biodeterioration, construction and finishing.
FRI wood testing and identification services — outlines specialist services when identification or quality is uncertain.

forest-teak-guide.title: Forest and Nigam Teak Wood: A Buyer's Guide for Doors and Frames
forest-teak-guide.excerpt: Understand forest and Nigam teak before buying a door or chaukhat. Check source records, heartwood, seasoning, defects and finished dimensions.
forest-teak-guide.summary: Understand forest and Nigam teak before buying a door or chaukhat. Check source records, heartwood, seasoning, defects and finished dimensions.
paragraphs: When a timber seller describes a piece as “forest teak” or “Nigam teak,” it is worth asking what that tells you about the actual wood. Is the source documented? Which lot did it come from? Is the section sound, properly seasoned and suitable for the door you want?

Genuine teak is Tectona grandis, known in India as sagwan. It is valued for its grain, workability, relatively low dimensional movement and naturally durable heartwood. Those advantages do not make every teak log the same grade.
This guide explains the source labels and the practical checks that matter when choosing teak for doors, windows and chaukhats.

sections.title: What do “forest teak” and “Nigam teak” mean?

blocks.text: “Forest teak” is used as an origin description. On its own, it does not document a tree's age, a grading standard or the condition of the timber.

“Nigam teak” usually refers to timber associated with a forest-corporation sales channel. The Uttar Pradesh Forest Corporation publishes timber-sale and depot information, and forest-corporation auctions provide lot-specific records.

A sales channel is not the same as a growing history. Timber sold through a corporation should not automatically be described as old-growth or naturally regenerated forest teak. Ask for the documentation relevant to the lot.

sections.title: What to ask about an auction-sourced lot

blocks.text: Useful information can include the species, depot, lot reference, sale or purchase record, dimensions, quantity and any stated category or grade.

Keep each claim tied to what the record actually establishes. A lot number may support traceability; it does not prove a finished door's moisture content. A size class does not automatically identify the tree's age.
Where timber changes hands after an auction, ask how the supplier's material relates to the source record. Do not infer provenance from the look of a log or from a photograph of an auction yard.

sections.title: Does UP or Uttarakhand origin guarantee quality?

blocks.text: No state name is a universal timber grade. Site conditions, individual trees, sawing, defects, drying and storage can all affect the sections that reach a workshop.

Distinguish the place of sale from the place where the tree grew. A depot in Uttar Pradesh or Uttarakhand is useful supply-chain information, but it does not by itself establish the growth origin of every lot.
For your door or chaukhat, the usable timber and its present condition are more informative than an unsupported regional ranking.

sections.title: How to assess the wood itself

blocks.text: Heartwood and sapwood
The darker inner heartwood generally has greater natural durability than the paler sapwood. Ask which portions will be included, especially in exposed components.
Sound heartwood is desirable, but a section with deep splits or decay should not be accepted simply because it is dark.
Grain and appearance
Teak commonly shows golden-brown to brown tones and straight or sometimes wavy grain. Sawing direction and surface preparation affect the pattern you see.

Choose visible boards with the finished design in mind. Matching colour can create a calm appearance; a strongly figured panel can be a feature. Neither choice proves the age or strength of the timber.
Defects and straightness
Inspect the full length of stiles and frame members, not just the ends. Look for twist, bow, deep checks, loose knots and damaged areas near joints or hardware.
Large logs do not guarantee large clear sections. The amount of sound timber left after defects and machining is part of the value.
Species identity

Colour, smell and an oily feel are useful clues, not definitive tests. Ask for the species on the quotation. If identity is disputed, a professional wood-identification service is more reliable than a social-media identification trick.

sections.title: Does older teak always perform better?

blocks.text: A mature tree may provide larger sections and different heartwood proportions, but age is only one factor. It does not remove defects or correct poor seasoning.
Likewise, timber stored for years is not necessarily ready to use. Storage conditions determine whether it stays dry and sound.
Ask whether an age claim is documented. If it is not, base the decision on the grade, heartwood, dimensions, defects and measured condition you can assess.

sections.title: Seasoning and moisture: the part a sample cannot show

blocks.text: Teak still absorbs and releases moisture. Its generally favourable dimensional behaviour reduces some risks but does not make a door immune to seasonal movement.

Ask for current readings across the relevant timber, the agreed moisture target and how the material is stored after drying. Thick frame sections need particular attention because a surface reading may not represent the core.

BIS IS 287 provides moisture-content recommendations according to purpose and climatic conditions. A single percentage should not be presented as correct for every home, exterior opening and air-conditioned room.
Air drying and kiln drying are preparation methods. Judge the result: suitable moisture condition, acceptable drying defects and proper conditioning before manufacture.

sections.title: Using forest or Nigam teak in joinery

blocks.text: Main and internal doors

Selected teak can suit panelled, carved and other solid-wood door designs. The board layout, joints and allowance for movement need to suit the opening. Exterior doors also need a suitable protective finish and weather detailing.
Windows
A timber window works as a system. The frame, sash, glass, seals, hardware and water-shedding details all matter. Teak cannot compensate for a sill or joint that holds water.
Frames and chaukhats
Confirm the finished section, rebate, clear opening and fixing details. Inspect long lengths for straightness and choose sound timber around hinge and lock positions.
Ask about wall-facing surfaces and floor junctions before installation, particularly where building work may expose the timber to wet materials.

sections.title: How durable is teak?

blocks.text: Teak heartwood is valued for natural decay resistance, but “termite-proof,” “waterproof” and “maintenance-free” are unsuitable promises. Sapwood, timber quality and exposure differ.
Good design and maintenance protect the investment. Keep water from collecting, monitor exposed edges and joints, and follow the coating manufacturer's care instructions.

sections.title: Teak, sal and sheesham: compare the intended use

blocks.text: These are different species. The table is a starting point for discussion, not a ranking or a guarantee for every board.

sections.title: What affects forest teak wood price?

blocks.text: Compare like-for-like material. A rate per cubic foot says little unless you know the grade, sizes, defects, moisture condition and usable recovery.
For a finished door, include construction, finish, hardware, delivery and installation in the quotation. The following factors help explain why two teak offers can differ.

rows: Documents that support the claimed origin
Its definition and the actual stock
Finished usable sizes, not just rough sizes
Amount and placement in the product
Appearance and suitability for each component
Current condition and the agreed target
Documented context; not a standalone grade

sections.title: Buying forest teak products from NORDWOOD

blocks.text: For a custom door, window or chaukhat, start with the opening and the intended exposure. NORDWOOD can discuss the available timber and design, arrange an on-site consultation and show wood samples during a workshop visit.

Ask for the agreed species, finished dimensions, finish and installation scope in the order. If forest-corporation provenance is important to your purchase, make the supporting documentation part of that discussion.

sections.title: Common questions

blocks.text: Is Nigam teak a separate species?
No. “Nigam” describes a sales or sourcing association, not a botanical species. Confirm that the timber is Tectona grandis.
Does Nigam teak mean an old tree?
No fixed age follows from the label. Ask what the individual lot records establish.
Is forest teak always better than plantation teak?
No. Compare actual grade, sections, heartwood, defects and preparation. Plantation and forest origin do not replace a quality assessment.
Can grain or colour prove the origin?
No. Appearance varies within teak and changes with cutting and finishing. Use documentation and, if necessary, professional identification.
Is auction-sourced timber ready for a door?
Not necessarily. Timber still needs appropriate conversion, selection, drying and conditioning before joinery.
What should I check before ordering a teak chaukhat?
Confirm the finished section, straightness, sound timber at joints and fixings, current moisture condition and installation details.

choosing-wood-with-the-whole-room-in-min.title: How to Choose the Right Wood for Doors and Windows
choosing-wood-with-the-whole-room-in-min.excerpt: Compare wood for doors, windows and chaukhats. Learn what to check for seasoning, grain, frame sizes, finishing and installation before you buy.
choosing-wood-with-the-whole-room-in-min.summary: Compare wood for doors, windows and chaukhats. Learn what to check for seasoning, grain, frame sizes, finishing and installation before you buy.
paragraphs: A door that looks good in a showroom still has to fit your home through hot summers, humid weather and years of daily use. Choosing the right wood starts with where it will be installed, then moves on to the condition of the timber and the way the whole assembly is made.

For most homeowners, the useful questions are straightforward: Will this door face rain? Is the wood properly seasoned? What are the finished dimensions? Who will measure, fit and finish it? Those answers often tell you more than a label such as “premium teak.”
This guide explains what to check when choosing wooden doors, windows and chaukhats, with practical considerations for homes in Lucknow and similar North Indian conditions.

sections.title: Start with exposure, not a favourite species

blocks.text: A sheltered bedroom door and a west-facing entrance need different specifications. Windows also need to shed water and maintain a good seal around the opening.
Before discussing wood, tell the manufacturer:

items: Whether the unit is indoors, under a porch or directly exposed to rain.
How much sunlight it receives.
Whether the room is regularly air-conditioned.
The opening size, door design and proposed hardware.
Whether you want a natural wood finish or a painted surface.

blocks.text: A bathroom entrance may be sheltered from direct water but still face high humidity. An external window may need more careful drainage and coating details than an indoor door made from the same timber.

sections.title: Understand what the wood name actually means

blocks.text: Teak

Genuine teak is Tectona grandis, also called sagwan. It is valued for its appearance, relatively low movement and naturally durable heartwood. Plantation teak, imported teak and Indian forest teak can all be the same species; those descriptions concern origin or growing conditions, not a guaranteed grade.
Indian sal or sakhu

Indian sal is Shorea robusta. It is a substantial hardwood often considered for door frames and other demanding work. Its weight and drying behaviour deserve attention, especially in large sections. A heavy door also needs suitable hinges, fixings and a sound frame.
Kapur and “Malaysian sal”

These names require a little more care. Kapur refers to Dryobalanops timber, while “Malaysian sal” is a market description that does not identify one consistent species. Ask for the botanical name or recognised timber group before comparing durability or price.
The USDA Wood Handbook and ICFRE's field-identification handbook are useful starting points for understanding why species, grade and individual timber condition should be considered together.

sections.title: Ask to see the actual timber

blocks.text: A polished sample shows a possible finish. It may not show the quality of the boards allocated to your order.

Where practical, look at the unpolished timber or representative samples. Sight along long pieces for bow or twist, inspect the ends for deep splits, and check areas where hinges, locks and joints will be cut. Small sound knots may suit a design; loose knots or deep cracks near a joint deserve closer assessment.
Colour and smell can offer clues, but they do not reliably authenticate a species. Ask for the identity and origin in writing.

sections.title: Make seasoning a measurable part of the order

blocks.text: Wood exchanges moisture with the surrounding air. If it is machined while too wet for its intended setting, later drying can affect fit and joints. Timber dried for a much drier environment can also move when installed somewhere humid.

“Kiln dried” describes a process, not the condition of every piece at delivery. Ask for the current moisture readings, how they were taken and the target agreed for your project. Measurements should account for the meter, species and section thickness.

There is no single ideal percentage for every Indian door or window. BIS IS 287 provides moisture-content recommendations for different purposes and climatic conditions. The manufacturer should select a suitable target rather than promise that one number works everywhere.

sections.title: Choose the construction as carefully as the material

blocks.text: A wide solid panel needs room to respond to humidity. Joints, panel layout, adhesives and hardware should suit the design and exposure.

Ask how the manufacturer will accommodate movement, what the finished thickness will be and how the door will be supported. For a large or double door, discuss leaf weight, hinges, locks, meeting edges and the frame together.

Solid timber, veneered doors, plywood-based products and other engineered assemblies are different constructions. Do not judge all engineered products by ordinary MDF: their moisture performance depends on the core, adhesive, grade and complete assembly.

sections.title: Give the frame equal attention

blocks.text: The chaukhat carries the door and transfers loads through its fixings. A well-made leaf cannot compensate for an undersized, twisted or badly fitted frame.

Confirm the finished frame section, rebate, wall thickness, fixing arrangement and door clearance before production. “Rough size” and “finished size” are not interchangeable; planing and profiling remove material.
At installation, the opening should be ready, the frame checked for square and plumb, and the timber protected from persistent moisture at masonry or floor junctions.

sections.title: Decide who will apply the finish

blocks.text: NORDWOOD supplies polished and unpolished products. An unpolished door gives you control over the final appearance, but it still needs a finishing plan before exposure and use.

Ask for a sample on the actual wood. A clear coating, stain or paint can change its appearance considerably. Exterior work needs a suitable exterior coating system, with attention to edges, end grain, joints and hardware cut-outs.
Follow the coating manufacturer's preparation and maintenance instructions. Adding oil or wax over an existing finish is not automatically appropriate.

sections.title: Compare complete quotations

blocks.text: A lower timber rate does not necessarily produce a lower finished-door cost. Compare:

items: Species or timber group and grade.
Finished sizes and construction.
Glass, hardware and accessories included.
Surface preparation and finishing.
Measurement, delivery and installation.
Agreed lead time, payment terms and after-sales arrangements.

blocks.text: For timber quoted by volume, compare the same units and whether sizes are rough or finished. For a finished product, compare the complete specification.

sections.title: Choosing with NORDWOOD

blocks.text: NORDWOOD makes custom wooden doors, windows and frames for customers in Lucknow. You can discuss the opening and design through an on-site consultation, visit the workshop to compare wood samples, and choose a polished or unpolished finish. Free installation is included with NORDWOOD products.

Bring your drawings, approximate opening sizes, photographs and preferred style to the discussion. That gives the team a clearer starting point for recommending a material and preparing a useful quotation.

sections.title: Common questions

blocks.text: Which wood is best for a main door?

There is no universal winner. Seasoned teak is a familiar choice, while other identified hardwoods can also be suitable. Exposure, heartwood, defects, construction, hardware and maintenance should guide the decision.
Is teak termite-proof?
No. Teak heartwood has natural resistance, but sapwood and individual material differ. Good building-level termite management and moisture control remain important.
Is sal suitable for chaukhat?
Sound, suitably seasoned sal can be a practical frame material. Inspect straightness, cracks, finished size and the sections around joints and fixings.
Should I choose kiln-dried wood?
Ask about the measured condition, not only the drying label. Correct drying, conditioning and storage matter whichever process is used.
Can I finish an unpolished door later?
Yes, but agree how it will be stored and when it will be sealed. Avoid leaving an unfinished exterior door exposed while other building work continues.

sources.title: USDA Forest Products Laboratory — Wood Handbook
BIS — IS 287 moisture-content recommendations
ICFRE — Field Identification of Selected Timbers of India

kapoor-sal-guide.title: Kapur Wood for Chaukhat: Properties, Uses and Buying Advice
kapoor-sal-guide.excerpt: Buying kapur or Kapoor Sal for a chaukhat? Understand its identity, termite resistance, seasoning, finished sizes and the checks that matter.
kapoor-sal-guide.summary: Buying kapur or Kapoor Sal for a chaukhat? Understand its identity, termite resistance, seasoning, finished sizes and the checks that matter.
paragraphs: If a quotation for your door frame says “Kapoor Sal,” start by asking which timber the supplier means. The name is used in the Indian timber trade, but it is not enough to identify a single botanical species.

When the material is confirmed as kapur, it belongs to the Dryobalanops group. It is different from Indian sal, or sakhu, which is Shorea robusta. Adding “sal” to a market name does not make two timbers the same.

This guide covers identified kapur timber and the checks that matter when buying it for a chaukhat, wooden door or window. The practical aim is to help you compare an actual specification, rather than choose on the name alone.

sections.title: Kapur and Indian sal: what is the difference?

blocks.text: Both are hardwoods used in construction and joinery, but their properties are not interchangeable. The comparison below applies to documented kapur; a supplier should confirm the identity of anything offered as “Kapoor Sal.”

rows: Dryobalanops timber; confirm a “Kapoor Sal” quotation
Southeast Asian supply; confirm the actual origin
South Asian supply; confirm the actual origin
Usually paler; inspect the actual section
Published group range: 575–815 kg/m³; condition matters
Generally substantial; varies with timber and moisture
Select grade and sections for the intended assembly
Select grade and sections for the intended assembly
Species and exposure matter; not termite-resistant
Durable heartwood; no blanket termite-proof claim
Frames, joinery and other construction uses
Frames, construction and other timber uses
Kapur; Kapoor/Kapoor Sal may need clarification

sections.title: What does kapur wood look like?

blocks.text: Kapur typically has reddish-brown heartwood and paler yellowish-brown sapwood. Its texture is relatively coarse, and grain may be straight, interlocked or spiral. Freshly cut timber can have a camphor-like smell.
Those features are useful observations, not a conclusive identification test. Colour changes with surface preparation and exposure, and a photograph cannot establish the exact species.
The STIDC Kapur profile gives a density range of 575–815 kg/m³. Treat this as a published reference for the timber group, not a measurement or grade certificate for your order.

sections.title: Is kapur a good choice for chaukhat?

blocks.text: Kapur is documented for door and window frames and other joinery. It can be a practical choice where the identified timber, drying quality and frame design suit the job.

For a chaukhat, ask to inspect the long members. Check straightness, end splits and the areas where joints, hinges and lock fittings will be cut. A defect in a short offcut may not matter; the same defect at a hinge position may.

Confirm the finished section after planing and rebating. A rough section sold as 4 inches by 2.5 inches will not necessarily retain those dimensions after machining. The size and orientation should suit the door, wall opening and fixing details, not just the supplier's available stock.

sections.title: What about doors and windows?

blocks.text: Door leaves

Identified, suitably prepared kapur can be considered for solid-wood or panelled doors. Match the board selection and construction to the leaf size and exposure. A heavy design also requires appropriate hardware and a frame that can carry it.
Window frames

Windows need to drain water and keep joints and glazing details protected. Species choice is only one part of the specification. Ask about the profile, seals, coating and maintenance plan, especially where rain reaches the frame directly.
Other uses

Kapur also has documented construction, flooring and furniture applications. That does not mean every board is suitable for every use: grade, defects, dimensions and treatment requirements still apply.

sections.title: Is kapur termite-resistant?

blocks.text: Do not buy kapur on a promise that it is termite-proof. Business Queensland's Kapur profile lists it as not termite-resistant. Decay durability and termite resistance are different properties.
Published durability ratings can also differ with species, test conditions and whether timber is above ground or in ground contact. A test classification is not a warranty for an installed door.

For a frame, discuss termite protection as part of the building and installation, together with any appropriate timber treatment. Keep timber away from persistent damp and maintain the protective finish.

sections.title: Seasoning: check the timber's condition now

blocks.text: Kapur needs controlled drying. A board can look dry on the surface while its moisture condition remains uneven, particularly in thicker sections.
Ask for current moisture readings, the method used and the agreed target for the service environment. The USDA guidance on drying explains why storage and conditioning after drying matter as well.
There is no universal moisture percentage for every chaukhat. An air-conditioned room, a sheltered entrance and an exposed window do not present identical conditions.

Air drying and kiln drying can both form part of preparation. What matters is whether the timber reaches an appropriate, reasonably uniform condition without unacceptable checks, distortion or drying stress.

sections.title: Tree age and years in storage are not the same thing

blocks.text: A claim that wood is “old” can refer to the tree or to time since sawing. Neither is a complete quality specification.

Timber that has spent years in a damp store may still need conditioning. Conversely, properly prepared material does not need an impressive age story to be useful. Inspect the timber and ask for evidence where age is part of the selling claim.

sections.title: A practical inspection before you order

items: Confirm Dryobalanops or the recognised timber identity on the quotation.
Ask for origin, grade and available source documentation.
Sight along the pieces for bow, crook and twist.
Check both faces and ends for splits, decay and insect damage.
Examine knots and grain around planned joints and fixings.
Confirm the heartwood and sapwood included.
Measure actual sizes and agree the finished dimensions.
Request moisture readings and the seasoning history.
Ask how the timber will be stored and protected before installation.

blocks.text: These checks work best on the actual stock or representative allocated pieces, rather than only on a polished sample.

sections.title: Why workmanship still matters

blocks.text: A frame has to remain square, hold its hardware and fit the wall opening. Accurate machining, suitable joints and careful fixing help turn timber into a useful assembly.

The same applies to finishing. Agree the preparation and coating for the actual exposure, including end grain and edges. If you order an unpolished product, decide who will finish it and how it will be protected until then.
For windows and exterior doors, a finish cannot compensate for a design that traps water.

sections.title: Kapur, teak, sal or sheesham?

blocks.text: Start with the application. Teak is commonly valued for its dimensional behaviour and heartwood durability. Sal is a substantial hardwood with different drying and working characteristics. Sheesham has its own grain, appearance and construction uses.

A meaningful comparison uses identified timber, equivalent finished sizes and a similar manufacturing specification. It should not compare the lowest rough-timber rate for one wood with a finished product price for another.

sections.title: What affects kapur wood price?

blocks.text: Species or timber group, grade, dimensions, clear usable lengths, defects, seasoning, transport and availability all affect a quotation. Larger pieces with fewer defects may produce more usable components, even if their initial rate is higher.

For a finished door or chaukhat, compare design, machining, joinery, hardware, finish, delivery and installation as well. Ask for those inclusions in writing; there is no reliable single price for every product sold as “Kapoor Sal.”

sections.title: Source documentation and responsible buying

blocks.text: Ask where the timber came from and what documentation supports the supply. If certification is claimed, check that it covers the supplier and the material being sold.
A country name, an attractive grain or the word “imported” does not by itself establish responsible sourcing.

sections.title: Planning a kapur chaukhat with NORDWOOD

blocks.text: Bring your opening dimensions, door design and exposure details to NORDWOOD. A workshop discussion can help you compare the available timber, understand the finished section and agree the finish and installation requirements.
For a useful quotation, specify the wood identity and finished product clearly. “Kapoor Sal frame” alone leaves too much open to interpretation.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions

blocks.text: Is Kapoor Sal the same as kapur?
It may be used that way in a quotation, but confirm the identity. This guide uses kapur for Dryobalanops timber.
Is kapur the same as Indian sal or sakhu?
No. Indian sal is Shorea robusta; kapur is Dryobalanops timber.
Is kapur suitable for door frames?
It has documented frame and joinery uses. Suitability depends on the particular timber, seasoning, dimensions, exposure and construction.
Can kapur be used outside?
Use an exposure-specific specification. Discuss durability, termite protection, finishing, drainage and maintenance rather than treating the species as automatically weatherproof.
Does kapur need kiln drying?
The requirement is an appropriate moisture condition, not a label alone. Air drying, kiln drying and subsequent conditioning should be selected for the timber and application.
How can I identify good kapur?
Confirm the identity through documentation, then inspect condition and dimensions. Smell and colour are clues, not proof.
